title: Acutely painful, hot, swollen left knee in a 70-year-old man with diabetes
desc: This station involves a focused joint pain history and examination of a 70-year-old retired engineer who comes to his GP with an acutely painful, hot, swollen left knee. He cannot bear weight. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, a urine dipstick and his most recent practice bloods. They recognise septic arthritis, arrange same-day hospital transfer for joint aspiration before antibiotics, plan the synovial fluid analysis and safety-net.
focus: Acute hot monoarthritis: a focused joint pain history and examination, recognising septic arthritis and arranging aspiration before antibiotics
stem: You are a medical student on your general practice rotation. Roger Sinclair, a 70-year-old man, has come to the practice with joint pain. He looks very uncomfortable, is grimacing and is holding his left knee slightly bent (about 20–30°), supported and still. Your GP supervisor has asked you to see him first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Sinclair and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his observations, his urine dipstick result and his most recent blood results from the practice record. Interpret them in a handover, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, outline your management including what you tell him, and name the key investigation (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Roger Sinclair, a 70-year-old retired engineer. You are in a lot of pain. You grimace, sit holding your left knee slightly bent (about 20–30°), supported and still, and will not stand on it. You are polite, but distracted by the pain. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "My knee is killing me. I can't even stand having my jeans touch it."

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Site: your left knee, the whole knee. It does not spread anywhere.
  • Onset: it started suddenly yesterday at about 3 pm, about 20 hours ago.
  • Character: "Sharp, throbbing, really intense."
  • Timing: constant, and it has got steadily worse since it started.
  • Worse: putting any weight on it, or any pressure at all, even your heavy jeans resting on it. Any movement of the knee.
  • Better: resting with the knee slightly bent on a pillow. Panadol did not help at all.
  • Severity: 10 out of 10. You cannot put weight on it or walk.
  • Swelling: the whole knee is swollen and red, not just a lump at the front of the kneecap.

Injury: if asked whether you have fallen or hurt your knee, say: "I haven't fallen on it or injured my knee at all." Only if asked specifically about cuts, wounds or breaks in the skin, or what you were doing before it started: two days ago you were working outdoors, knelt down and knelt on an old dirty nail sticking out of a board. It went into the front of your left knee, just below the kneecap. It bled a little. You washed it and put a bandaid on it and did not think about it again.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Fever: last night you felt hot and then cold, shivered under the blankets and woke drenched in sweat. You have not taken your temperature. You feel generally unwell and have not felt like eating today.
  • No pain or swelling in any other joint today. No back pain.
  • No cough, no urinary symptoms, no skin infections elsewhere, no tooth problems, no diarrhoea, no sore or red eyes, no rash.
  • No calf pain.

Questions about other causes (only if asked):

  • You have never had gout or a sudden hot, swollen joint before, and never a painful big toe. You have no lumps on your ears or elbows. You take no fluid tablets.
  • You have been married for 45 years and have had no other sexual partners. No penile discharge, no burning when passing urine.
  • You take no blood thinners and have no bleeding problems.
  • You have no joint replacements and have never had an injection or operation on either knee. You have never used IV drugs. You have never taken steroid tablets.
  • You have not travelled overseas.
  • Your usual arthritis: both knees ache, worse at the end of the day, with some morning stiffness that settles within half an hour. "This is nothing like it. It's much, much worse."

Past medical history: osteoarthritis in both knees and at the base of both thumbs since about age 65. "I use a walking aid sometimes when it's playing up." Type 2 diabetes for 3 years. "The GP said last time my sugar test was a bit high." You do not check your sugars at home. No other illnesses, no operations.

Medications: metformin, one tablet in the morning and one at night. Occasional Panadol for your arthritis; you took 2 tablets yesterday evening and 2 this morning, with no effect. No other medicines.

Allergies: none.

Tetanus (only if asked): "I had the full course of tetanus needles at school, it's in my old record book, and a tetanus booster when I cut my hand on a fence about 15 years ago."

Family history: your mother died at 95 and your father died at 93; he had osteoarthritis. Your brother is well. You have two healthy daughters. No one in your family has had gout or inflammatory arthritis.

Social history:

  • You smoked half a pack a day from age 30 to 40 and none since.
  • Alcohol about once a fortnight, a couple of glasses of wine.
  • You are a retired engineer. Normally you walk to the shops and the park.
  • You eat a healthy diet and cook with your wife.
  • You live with your wife in a small house. Your wife and daughters live in the same city. Your wife drove you here today.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "I'm not sure what this could be. It doesn't feel like my usual joint pain, it's much, much worse. I haven't fallen on, or injured, my knee at all."
  • Impact: "The pain is just so bad that I can't concentrate on anything, and I can't do any jobs, or even go to the grocery store, because I can't walk on it."
  • Concerns: "If this doesn't go away, how will I be able to survive and do my usual activities? I'm worried something serious is going on because it is just so painful."
  • Expectations: you hope for something stronger for the pain and to be back on your feet.

Response to the candidate: if the candidate tries to bend your knee firmly, cry out and pull away. If they explain first and are gentle, you let them look and feel, but you will not let them bend it more than a little. If asked something not covered here, give a realistic answer that fits the story.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: unwell-looking, flushed and sweaty, grimacing. He is holding the left knee slightly bent (about 20–30°), supported and still, and refuses to stand. Alert and oriented.
  • Vital signs (practice nurse, 10:40): temperature 38.4 °C; HR 104 beats/min, regular; BP 138/82 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 97% on room air; finger-prick glucose 13.8 mmol/L.
  • Left knee, inspection: diffusely swollen, with loss of the normal hollows beside the patella. The skin over the whole knee is red. A 3 mm scabbed puncture wound lies 2 cm below the lower pole of the patella, just medial to the patellar tendon, with 3 cm of surrounding redness. No pus, no visible foreign body, no red streaks up the thigh, no scars.
  • Left knee, palpation: clearly hotter than the right knee. Large effusion: positive patellar tap. Tender all around the joint, including both joint lines, not just over the front of the patella. No separate fluctuant swelling in front of the patella or over the patellar tendon.
  • Left knee, movement: he will only move it actively about 10° from the slightly bent position he holds it in. Any passive movement beyond a few degrees in any direction causes severe pain, and the examiner advises not to force it. Gait not testable: he cannot bear weight.
  • Right knee: bony enlargement and crepitus, no effusion, not warm, flexion to 120°, non-tender.
  • Other joints: squaring at the base of both thumbs. No tophi on the ears, elbows or hands. Both first MTP joints are normal. No other swollen or tender joints. Left hip: full, pain-free passive rotation. Left ankle normal.
  • Nodes and skin: one tender 1 cm left inguinal node. No rash and no pustules. Eyes not red. No mouth ulcers.
  • Legs and feet: left calf soft and non-tender. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses present on both sides. Monofilament sensation intact. No foot ulcers.
  • Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdomen: dual heart sounds, no murmur. Chest clear. Abdomen soft, non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms the patient's identity, and gains consent before examining, asking about pain first.
Acknowledges his severe pain and distress early, examines gently without forcing the knee, and uses plain language throughout.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: left knee only, no radiation.
Onset and course: sudden, yesterday about 3 pm (about 20 hours ago), constant and getting worse.
Character and severity: sharp, throbbing, intense, 10/10.
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse with weight-bearing or any pressure (even jeans), better resting with the knee slightly bent on a pillow, no relief from Panadol.
Function: cannot bear weight or walk, cannot do jobs or go to the shops.

check.x: Asks specifically about a break in the skin or what he was doing before the pain started, and finds he knelt on a dirty nail outdoors 2 days ago, even though he says he has not fallen or injured the knee.
Asks about fever, rigors, sweats and feeling unwell, and finds he had shivers and drenching sweats last night.
Screens for other causes of an acute hot knee:
check.d: Source marking: full credit for asking 3 or more features of 3 or more differentials. Credit 3 of the 5 sub-items for full marks.

kids.x: Gout or pseudogout: previous attacks, painful big toe, tophi, diet, alcohol, fluid tablets.
Gonococcal or reactive arthritis: sexual history, urethral discharge or dysuria, rash, recent diarrhoea or urinary infection, sore red eyes.
Trauma or haemarthrosis: fall or twisting injury, anticoagulants or a bleeding tendency.
OA flare: compares this with his usual OA pain and stiffness, and asks about other joints.
Septic bursitis: whether the whole knee is swollen or only a lump over the front of the kneecap.

check.x: Asks about risk factors for joint infection: diabetes and its control, immunosuppression or steroids, a joint replacement, recent joint injection or surgery, IV drug use, and infection elsewhere (skin, urine, chest, teeth).
check.d: Credit if 4 or more of the 6 risk-factor areas are asked, including diabetes and infection elsewhere.

check.x: Past medical history: OA in both knees and thumb bases since about 65, using a walking aid at times, and type 2 diabetes for 3 years.
Medications and allergies: metformin and occasional Panadol; no known drug allergies (asked because he will need antibiotics).
check.d: Credit if the medication list and allergy status are both obtained.

check.x: Asks about tetanus immunisation: full course at school (in his record book), last booster about 15 years ago.
Family history: asks briefly (father had OA; no gout or inflammatory arthritis).

Social history: ex-smoker (half a pack a day from 30 to 40), alcohol once a fortnight, retired engineer, usually walks to the shops and park, lives with his wife in a small house with family in the same city.
check.d: Credit if smoking, alcohol, usual function or mobility, and home supports are covered.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: this is much worse than his usual OA, he fears something serious, and he worries about coping with his usual activities.
Examination
Requests vital signs and a finger-prick glucose, and identifies fever (38.4 °C), tachycardia (104), normal BP, RR and SpO2, and a glucose of 13.8 mmol/L.
General inspection: unwell, flushed and sweaty, grimacing, holding the left knee slightly bent (about 20–30°), supported and still, unable to bear weight; alert.
Inspects and compares both knees: diffuse swelling, redness, the puncture wound below the patella with surrounding redness, and no red streaks up the thigh or surgical scars.

Palpates the knee for warmth compared with the other side, effusion (patellar tap or bulge test) and where it is tender, and identifies a joint effusion (rather than an isolated swelling in front of the patella).

kids.x: States that a joint effusion with tenderness all around the joint points to an intra-articular problem rather than bursitis.

check.x: Assesses active movement, then passive movement gently without forcing: severely restricted and painful in every direction.
Examines other joints: the joint above and below (left hip and ankle), the right knee (OA), the hands (thumb bases, tophi) and the first MTP joints.
Looks for spread and for another source: inguinal nodes, ascending lymphangitis, rash or pustules, red eyes, a heart murmur, and the distal pulses and sensation in the leg.
Interpretation

Observations: fever rising from 38.4 to 38.7 °C with a rigor, and HR 104 rising to 108, with normal BP, RR, SpO2 and alertness. Reads this as a systemic response to infection with possible bacteraemia, without organ dysfunction or shock, and with fever and heart rate rising he needs hospital today.

Glucose and urine: BGL 13.8 with glucosuria (2+) and no ketones means hyperglycaemia from acute infection on top of known diabetes, without ketosis. No leukocytes or nitrites, so a urinary source is unlikely.

Practice bloods: HbA1c 7.6% (60 mmol/mol) is above the usual target of 7% or less (53 mmol/mol), so diabetes control is suboptimal and a risk factor for infection. Normal renal function (eGFR 72) is a baseline for antibiotic dosing and metformin.
Concludes that an acute hot, swollen monoarthritis with fever after a skin puncture in a man with diabetes and OA is septic arthritis until proven otherwise.

Gives and weighs at least 3 differentials with a reason against each: crystal arthritis (gout or CPPD; can coexist, excluded only by aspiration), septic prepatellar or infrapatellar bursitis (against: true effusion, pain on all movement, no prebursal swelling), gonococcal or reactive arthritis (against: monogamous, no discharge, diarrhoea, rash or eye symptoms), OA flare or haemarthrosis (against: fever, no injury, no anticoagulants).
check.d: Credit 3 or more differentials, each with a reason.

check.x: Management
Arranges same-day urgent transfer to hospital, not outpatient tests or a review appointment:

kids.x: Phones the orthopaedic or ED registrar with a verbal handover.
Sends a written referral: timeline, nail puncture, observations, medicines, allergies, and that no antibiotics have been given.
Arranges ambulance transport, because he cannot bear weight and is febrile and tachycardic.

check.x: Does not start antibiotics in the practice, because the joint must be aspirated first so the culture is not lost. States the exception: if he develops signs of organ dysfunction or shock (SBP ≤100 or any red-zone observation, RR ≥22, new confusion or drowsiness, falling SpO2), call 000 and give antibiotics immediately, after blood cultures only if they can be taken without delay, without waiting for aspiration.
Keeps him nil by mouth (possible theatre), offers analgesia (e.g. an opioid) and rests the knee in the position of comfort.
Diabetes: tells the hospital about his hyperglycaemia, and states that metformin is usually withheld while he is acutely unwell and his glucose monitored.
check.d: Credit if the BGL and metformin are flagged in the ISBAR.

check.x: Tetanus: a tetanus-prone puncture wound 5 years or more since his last dose needs a tetanus-containing vaccine booster. Tetanus immunoglobulin is not needed because he has had 3 or more doses. Also credit a candidate who checks the dose history, and who would give tetanus immunoglobulin if 3 doses cannot be confirmed.
check.d: Credit if raised in the history or anywhere in Part 2.

check.x: States the hospital plan: after aspiration and blood cultures, empirical IV antibiotics per eTG (e.g. flucloxacillin 2 g IV 6-hourly), adjusted to Gram stain and culture, and urgent orthopaedic washout.
check.d: Credit if given in the ISBAR Recommendation, the management answer or the investigation answer; the exact dose is not required.

check.x: Explains in plain words: probably an infection in the joint; he must go to hospital today, and that he goes by ambulance, nil by mouth; the needle test comes before antibiotics; he may need the joint washed out. Answers his request for antibiotics at home.
Names joint aspiration as the immediate investigation, done before antibiotics and without delay, with blood cultures.
Requests synovial fluid analysis:

kids.x: Gram stain, and culture with sensitivities.

check.x: Safety netting
Arranges repeat observations by the nurse while he waits for the ambulance, with escalation if they worsen.

Names at least 3 specific red flags for him, his wife and staff while he waits for the ambulance: confusion or drowsiness, faintness or light-headedness, breathlessness, cold or mottled skin, rapidly spreading redness.

part2.lead: The practice nurse took Mr Sinclair's observations on arrival and again 25 minutes later, and tested his urine. Here are those results and his most recent blood results from the practice record.
part2.patient:
When the candidate explains the plan, Mr Sinclair asks, if not already covered:

  • "Can't you just give me some antibiotics and I'll rest it at home?"

Ask the other two only if the candidate finishes with time to spare; they are not scored: "Are they going to put a needle in my knee? Will I need an operation?" and "Will I be able to walk properly again?"

He agrees to go to hospital once the candidate explains that the needle test has to come before antibiotics.

handover.label: Observations (practice nurse)
handover.result: Room air throughout. Finger-prick glucose on arrival. Repeat set at 11:05 while waiting to be seen by the GP.
handover.model:
Read: at 10:40, temperature 38.4 °C, HR 104 regular, BP 138/82, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, alert, pain 10/10, finger-prick glucose 13.8 mmol/L. At 11:05 the temperature is 38.7 °C after a rigor, HR 108, BP 134/80, RR 20, SpO2 97%, still alert. The practice has no track-and-trigger chart. Physiologically he has a fever and a tachycardia, but on an adult Between the Flags chart only the 11:05 temperature (38.7 °C) falls in the yellow zone. HR 104–108, BP, RR 18–20 and SpO2 97% are in the normal zone, and nothing is in the red zone. He has a fever and tachycardia (he would meet the older SIRS criteria) but no organ dysfunction, so he does not meet the current definition of sepsis.

For Mr Sinclair: a rising fever with rigors and tachycardia is a systemic response to infection and suggests possible bacteraemia. With a normal BP, normal RR and SpO2 and normal consciousness, there is no sign of organ dysfunction or septic shock.

What it changes: his fever and heart rate are rising and he needs hospital today, by ambulance. Because he has no signs of organ dysfunction or shock, antibiotics wait for joint aspiration in hospital. The nurse repeats his observations while he waits. If he develops signs of organ dysfunction or shock (SBP ≤100 or any red-zone observation, RR ≥22, new confusion or drowsiness, falling SpO2), call 000 and give antibiotics immediately, after blood cultures only if they can be taken without delay, without waiting for aspiration.

handover.label: Urine dipstick
handover.result: Midstream urine, dipstick tested in the practice at 10:50.
handover.model:
Read: glucose 2+, with ketones, leukocytes, nitrites, blood and protein all negative. Specific gravity 1.025 and pH 5.5.

For Mr Sinclair: glucosuria matches his finger-prick glucose of 13.8: hyperglycaemia driven by acute infection on top of his type 2 diabetes. Negative ketones mean no ketosis. Negative leukocytes and nitrites make a urinary source of infection unlikely. A specific gravity at the high end of normal suggests he has drunk little today, although glucosuria also raises specific gravity.

What it changes: the hospital team needs to know his glucose so they can monitor it and review his metformin while he is unwell. It supports the knee, with its puncture wound, as the source.

handover.label: Most recent bloods (practice record, 3 months ago)
handover.result: Routine diabetes review bloods collected 3 months ago. There are no more recent results.
handover.model:
Read: HbA1c 7.6% (60 mmol/mol), above the usual general target of 7% or less (53 mmol/mol). Sodium, potassium and creatinine are normal, with an eGFR of 72.

For Mr Sinclair: diabetes control is suboptimal, which increases his risk of infection. Today's glucose of 13.8 is higher than this HbA1c would predict, which fits stress hyperglycaemia from the acute infection. His renal function was normal 3 months ago.

What it changes: these results are 3 months old. They give the hospital a baseline but do not replace today's FBC, CRP, ESR, UEC, LFT and blood cultures, which are taken in hospital and must not be waited for in the practice. Normal renal function is useful for antibiotic dosing. After recovery, the GP should review his diabetes control.

ask: You are now calling the orthopaedic registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Mr Sinclair, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Mr Sinclair now, here in general practice, including what you would tell him before he leaves for the hospital.
What is the most important immediate investigation for Mr Sinclair, and what would you ask the laboratory to do with the sample?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student at the practice, with my GP supervisor. Roger Sinclair, 70.
  • Situation: acutely hot, swollen, painful left knee for 20 hours. He cannot bear weight and has a fever. Likely septic arthritis. Requesting same-day assessment and aspiration.
  • Background: knelt on a dirty nail 2 days ago, causing a puncture below the patella. Type 2 diabetes on metformin (HbA1c 7.6% and normal renal function 3 months ago). OA of both knees. No prosthesis. No allergies.
  • Assessment: temperature 38.4 rising to 38.7 °C with a rigor, HR 104 to 108, BP 134/80, RR 20, SpO2 97% RA, alert: systemic infection, not shocked. BGL 13.8, urine glucose 2+, no ketones, no UTI.
  • Recommendation: please accept today for aspiration before antibiotics, blood cultures, IV antibiotics and washout. Coming by ambulance, nil by mouth, no antibiotics given.

Most likely: septic arthritis of the left knee from direct inoculation. For it: acute single hot, swollen joint with an effusion, 10/10 pain on any movement, unable to bear weight, fever with rigors, tachycardia, a nail puncture 2 days earlier, diabetes, pre-existing OA and age 70.

  • Gout or pseudogout: can look identical and can coexist with infection. Against gout: no previous attacks, no tophi, no diuretics, normal first MTPs. Pseudogout (CPPD) is common in an OA knee at 70 and cannot be excluded clinically; only crystals on aspiration distinguish it, and crystals do not exclude coexisting infection. The nail puncture and rigors favour infection.
  • Septic prepatellar or superficial infrapatellar bursitis: the wound overlies the infrapatellar region. Against it: true joint effusion, pain on all movement, no swelling in front of the patella.
  • Gonococcal or reactive arthritis: monogamous, no discharge, diarrhoea, rash or eye symptoms.
  • OA flare or haemarthrosis: against it: fever, much worse than his usual pain, no injury, no anticoagulants.

1. Same-day hospital transfer: phone the orthopaedic (or ED) registrar and send a written referral. Ambulance, because he cannot bear weight and is febrile and tachycardic. Not outpatient tests.
  2. No antibiotics in the practice: no organ dysfunction or shock, so aspiration comes first. If SBP ≤100, RR ≥22, new confusion or drowsiness, or falling SpO2: 000, and antibiotics immediately (after blood cultures only if they can be taken without delay), not waiting for aspiration.
  3. Nil by mouth (possible theatre). Analgesia (e.g. an opioid). Rest the knee.
  4. Diabetes: flag BGL 13.8. Metformin is usually withheld while he is acutely unwell, and his glucose monitored.
  5. Tetanus booster (tetanus-prone, last dose 15 years ago); no immunoglobulin.
  6. Tell him: likely a joint infection; the needle test must come before antibiotics, so antibiotics at home are not safe; he may need an operation to wash out the joint. Ambulance to hospital, nothing to eat, the hospital team is expecting him. The nurse repeats his observations while he waits. Tell staff at once about confusion or drowsiness, faintness, breathlessness, cold or mottled skin, or spreading redness.

• Joint aspiration (arthrocentesis) of the left knee, before antibiotics, without delay, in hospital today, with blood cultures taken at the same time.
  • Synovial fluid:
    • Appearance: turbid or purulent in sepsis.
    • Gram stain, culture and sensitivities.
    • White cell count and differential.
    • Crystals on polarised light microscopy (crystals do not exclude infection).

ddx.dx: Septic arthritis of the left knee from direct inoculation
ddx.for: Sudden single hot, swollen knee with an effusion, pain on any movement, unable to bear weight, fever with rigors and tachycardia, a dirty nail puncture 2 days earlier, diabetes and pre-existing OA.

ddx.dx: Acute crystal arthritis (gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition)
ddx.for: Sudden, exquisitely painful hot knee with an effusion in a 70-year-old with OA, where crystal arthritis can cause fever.
ddx.against: Against gout: no previous attacks, no tophi, no diuretics, normal first MTPs. Pseudogout (CPPD) is common in an OA knee at 70 and cannot be excluded clinically; only crystals on aspiration distinguish it, and crystals do not exclude coexisting infection. The nail puncture and rigors favour infection.

ddx.dx: Septic prepatellar or superficial infrapatellar bursitis
ddx.for: Kneeling injury with a puncture over the infrapatellar region and local redness.
ddx.against: A true joint effusion with tenderness all around the joint, pain on any movement and no separate swelling in front of the patella.

ddx.for: Acute monoarthritis of the knee with fever.
ddx.against: Married and monogamous for 45 years, with no discharge, dysuria, rash or tenosynovitis.

ddx.for: Acute inflammatory arthritis of a large joint of the leg.
ddx.against: No recent diarrhoea or urinary infection, no eye symptoms, no back pain, and a fever with rigors.

ddx.for: Known OA of both knees since about 65.
ddx.against: He says it is much, much worse than his usual pain, with fever, a hot red joint and inability to bear weight.

guide:
The station is set in general practice at about 10:55. In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. The vital signs are the practice nurse's 10:40 set. Mr Sinclair denies any fall or knee injury. He reveals the nail only if the candidate asks about cuts, wounds or breaks in the skin, or what he was doing beforehand. This is the key history trap. For item 8, give full credit for 3 or more features of 3 or more differentials (the source marking).

In Part 2, hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Mr Sinclair puts his first question while the candidate explains the plan; the other two only if time remains, and they are not scored. Credit items 38 and 39 if aspiration and the synovial fluid tests are given in the ISBAR or the management answer. Items 34 and 35 may be credited from the ISBAR or the history. A candidate who would give oral antibiotics and review tomorrow, or order outpatient bloods and wait, should not receive item 31 or 32.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain, uncovers the nail puncture despite his denial of injury, and asks about fever and risk factors. They screen gout, gonococcal and reactive arthritis, trauma and bursitis, and examine the knee gently, distinguishing an effusion from bursitis. In Part 2 they read the worsening fever and tachycardia as systemic infection without shock. They arrange same-day ambulance transfer with a phone handover, withhold antibiotics until the joint is aspirated (unless he develops organ dysfunction or shock), keep him nil by mouth and address tetanus and his diabetes. They name aspiration with Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals as the immediate investigation, and give specific red flags.

A borderline candidate accepts "no injury" and misses the nail, calls it an OA flare or gout, or forces the knee through a range of movement. They may start oral antibiotics in the practice, plan a routine X-ray and review, or forget that aspiration must come before antibiotics.
explain:
Diagnosis: septic arthritis of the left knee

Septic arthritis presents as an acute, single, hot, swollen, painful joint. The patient usually has a fever and cannot bear weight, and holds the joint still in the most comfortable position, resisting any movement. The knee is involved in about half of cases. Bacteria reach the joint either through the blood (bacteraemia) or by direct inoculation through wounds, bites or surgery. Mr Sinclair knelt on a dirty nail 2 days before the pain began, which is direct inoculation, and he has several risk factors: age 70, type 2 diabetes with suboptimal control, and pre-existing OA. Other risk factors are immunosuppression, IV drug use, bacteraemia, a prosthetic joint, and recent joint surgery or intra-articular injection. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism. Septic arthritis can destroy cartilage within days and can cause sepsis, so it is an emergency.

The history trap is that he says he has not injured his knee. Patients often do not count a small puncture as an injury, so always ask directly about cuts, wounds and what they were doing beforehand.

Differentials of an acute hot monoarthritis

  • Gout and pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition): can look identical, with fever, and can coexist with infection. Ask about previous attacks, the first MTP joint, tophi, diet, alcohol and diuretics.
  • Septic bursitis: prepatellar or superficial infrapatellar bursitis after kneeling causes a superficial swelling at the front of the knee, often with relatively preserved knee movement and no true effusion.
  • Gonococcal arthritis: usually younger, sexually active adults, often with migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis and pustular skin lesions.
  • Reactive arthritis: follows gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, sometimes with conjunctivitis or urethritis.
  • Trauma and haemarthrosis: injury, anticoagulants, bleeding disorders.
  • OA flare: a diagnosis of exclusion when there is fever and a hot joint.
  • Lyme arthritis is not relevant in Australia.

Interpreting the Part 2 results

  • Observations: fever rising to 38.7 °C with a rigor and HR above 100 show a systemic response to infection. His normal BP, RR, SpO2 and consciousness mean there is no organ dysfunction or shock. His fever and heart rate are rising, which makes same-day hospital care more urgent, not less.
  • Glucose and urine: stress hyperglycaemia (13.8 mmol/L, glucose 2+) without ketones. No leukocytes or nitrites, so a urinary source is unlikely.
  • Practice bloods: HbA1c 7.6% (60 mmol/mol) is above the general target of 7% (53 mmol/mol) or less, a risk factor for infection. Normal renal function 3 months ago is a baseline only. Today's bloods are done in hospital.

The immediate investigation: aspirate before antibiotics

Aspirate the joint without delay, before antibiotics, so that culture can identify the organism, and take blood cultures at the same time. Synovial fluid analysis:

  • Appearance: turbid or purulent.
  • White cell count and differential: often above 50 000 × 106/L (50 × 109/L) with more than 90% neutrophils.
  • Gram stain: may be negative even when the joint is infected.
  • Culture and sensitivities: the definitive test.
  • Crystals on polarised light microscopy: gout crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent; CPPD crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent. Crystals do not exclude coexisting infection.

Bloods: FBC (white cell count), CRP, ESR, UEC and LFT. Normal inflammatory markers do not exclude septic arthritis.

Management

In general practice: this cannot be managed in the practice. Arrange same-day transfer to hospital with a phone call to the orthopaedic or ED registrar and a written referral. Use an ambulance, because he cannot bear weight and is febrile. Do not start antibiotics before aspiration in a patient who is not shocked, because this can make the cultures falsely negative. If he develops signs of organ dysfunction or shock (SBP ≤100 or any red-zone observation, RR ≥22, new confusion or drowsiness, falling SpO2), call 000 and give antibiotics immediately, after blood cultures only if they can be taken without delay, without waiting for aspiration (ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard).

Before transfer:

  • Keep him nil by mouth, because he may need theatre.
  • Offer analgesia (e.g. an opioid such as IM/IV morphine, or oral with a sip of water, as the GP decides), noting he has taken paracetamol 2 g in the past 24 hours (1 g last evening, 1 g this morning).
  • Tell the hospital about his hyperglycaemia. Metformin is usually withheld while he is acutely unwell.
  • Manage the tetanus-prone wound. At 5 years or more since his last dose he needs a tetanus-containing vaccine. Tetanus immunoglobulin is not needed because he has had 3 or more documented doses; if 3 doses could not be confirmed, he would also need tetanus immunoglobulin (Australian Immunisation Handbook).

In hospital (eTG):

  • Plain X-ray of the left knee (baseline, retained foreign body, gas), without delaying aspiration.
  • After aspiration and blood cultures, empirical IV antibiotics for native joint septic arthritis in adults: flucloxacillin 2 g IV 6-hourly. Alternatives are used for penicillin allergy or MRSA risk.
  • Antibiotics are adjusted to the Gram stain and culture, and the duration is set by the treating team.
  • Urgent orthopaedic washout (arthroscopic or open), sometimes repeated.
  • Then mobilisation with physiotherapy.

Safety netting and follow-up

  • While waiting for the ambulance: the nurse repeats his observations, and he, his wife and staff watch for confusion or drowsiness, faintness or light-headedness, breathlessness, cold or mottled skin, or rapidly spreading redness. Ambulance to hospital, nothing to eat; the hospital team is expecting him. His wife follows with his medicines list.
  • After discharge, return urgently if fever, increasing knee pain or swelling, or wound redness comes back.
  • After discharge, the GP reviews:
    • completion of the antibiotic course
    • knee function and rehabilitation
    • diabetes control
    • the tetanus record.
points: An acute, single hot, swollen joint with fever is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. The knee is involved in about half of cases.
Ask directly about breaks in the skin: patients who knelt on a nail or were bitten often say they have not injured the joint.
Diabetes, age, pre-existing joint disease, immunosuppression, a prosthetic joint and recent joint injection or surgery all raise the risk.

Aspirate the joint before antibiotics, with blood cultures. Request appearance, Gram stain, culture with sensitivities, white cell count with differential, and crystals (gout: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent; CPPD: rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent). A negative Gram stain or the presence of crystals does not exclude infection.

In general practice, arrange same-day hospital transfer and do not give antibiotics first unless the patient has signs of organ dysfunction or shock. Keep the patient nil by mouth for possible washout.
Treat a dirty puncture wound as tetanus-prone: give a booster if it is 5 years or more since the last dose.
